name: The Picture Theory of Language
statement: A meaningful sentence is a picture of a possible fact, sharing its logical structure.
statementAccent: a picture of a possible fact
meaning: The picture theory of language, or picture theory of the proposition, is the account of language and meaning in Ludwig Wittgenstein's early work, the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, written during the First World War and published in German in 1921 and in English in 1922. It holds that a meaningful proposition is a picture, or model, of a possible state of affairs: a proposition represents reality by sharing a logical form with the possible fact it depicts. The elements or names in the proposition go proxy for objects in the world, and the arrangement of those elements mirrors the arrangement of the objects in the state of affairs, so that a proposition is a kind of logical picture whose sense is the possible situation it depicts. A proposition is true if that state of affairs obtains and false if it does not. What a picture must have in common with reality in order to depict it Wittgenstein called logical, or pictorial, form, and he held that this form can be shown but not said. The theory carries strong consequences drawn out in the Tractatus: only propositions that picture possible states of affairs, the propositions of natural science, can be said with sense, while the pronouncements of ethics, aesthetics, and metaphysics, and even the propositions of the Tractatus itself, are strictly nonsense, leading to the famous closing injunction that whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent. Wittgenstein later abandoned the picture theory for the use theory of meaning.
mechanism: The picture theory explains how a proposition can represent reality and be true or false. Wittgenstein starts from the idea that the world is the totality of facts, not of things, and that facts are configurations of objects. A proposition depicts a possible fact by being itself a fact, an arrangement of signs, that shares a structure with the situation it represents. The names in a fully analyzed proposition stand in for objects, and the way the names are combined pictures the way the objects would be combined in the state of affairs; representation is thus by structural isomorphism, a matching of logical form, much as a musical score can represent a piece of music or a model made of toy figures can represent an arrangement of real things. The sense of the proposition is the possible state of affairs it depicts, and its truth value depends on whether that state of affairs actually obtains: true if it does, false if it does not. This account fixes the limits of what can be meaningfully said. Only propositions that picture possible configurations of objects have sense, which for Wittgenstein means the factual propositions of natural science. The logical form that a proposition shares with reality cannot itself be pictured or stated, only shown, which underlies the distinction between showing and saying. Consequently the attempts of ethics, aesthetics, religion, and traditional metaphysics to state truths that are not pictures of contingent facts come out as nonsense, and Wittgenstein applies this even to the Tractatus, whose reader is told to throw away the ladder after climbing it, recognizing its own propositions as nonsensical.

examples.text: A proposition depicts a possible state of affairs by sharing its logical form, as a model or a musical score represents its subject.
The names in a proposition stand for objects, and their arrangement mirrors the arrangement of objects in the pictured fact.
Only propositions picturing possible facts can be said, so whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.

variants.name: Showing versus saying

whyItMatters: The picture theory of language is the centerpiece of the Tractatus, one of the most influential and enigmatic works of twentieth-century philosophy, and it gave a bold, unified answer to the question of how language can represent the world. By analyzing meaningful propositions as logical pictures that share a form with the possible facts they depict, Wittgenstein offered a powerful account of representation, truth, and the limits of what can be said, and he drew from it a striking view of philosophy itself: that most traditional philosophical claims, along with ethics and metaphysics, transgress the limits of sense and are nonsense, however important the matters they gesture at. The theory shaped the logical positivists, who took over its criterion for meaningful discourse and its hostility to metaphysics, and its distinction between showing and saying continues to provoke discussion. The picture theory is also historically pivotal as the view the later Wittgenstein came to reject, in favor of meaning as use, so that understanding it is essential to grasping the great turn in his thought and in the philosophy of language more broadly. As the early Wittgenstein's account of the proposition as a picture of reality, it is a landmark of modern philosophy.

limits: The picture theory is profound but was ultimately rejected by its own author. In the Philosophical Investigations, the later Wittgenstein abandoned it in favor of the use theory of meaning, language-games, and forms of life, criticizing the referential, Augustinian picture that the Tractatus partly embodied and arguing that treating every meaningful proposition as a picture of a fact distorts the many other things language does. The theory also faces internal strains, most famously the self-application problem: by its own criterion the propositions of the Tractatus, which are not pictures of contingent facts, come out as nonsense, which is why Wittgenstein tells the reader to throw away the ladder, but how a book of nonsense can nonetheless convey understanding remains deeply contested, dividing resolute from more traditional interpretations. The relegation of ethics, aesthetics, and metaphysics to the unsayable is likewise controversial. Some historical and textual details reward care, such as the 1921 German and 1922 English publication, the numbered propositions, and the different standard translations of the closing proposition seven. So the picture theory robustly explains representation as logical picturing, understood as a landmark account beset by the self-application problem and superseded by Wittgenstein's own later philosophy.
misreadings: The picture theory does not claim that sentences resemble the world in a visual or literal way; the picturing is a sharing of logical form, a structural isomorphism, not a physical likeness. Its verdict that ethics and metaphysics are nonsense is not a claim that they are unimportant, since Wittgenstein thought the unsayable mattered greatly, only that they cannot be put into meaningful propositions. And the theory is not Wittgenstein's final view, since he later rejected it, so treating picturing as visual resemblance, as dismissing ethics as trivial, or as his settled position, misreads the early Wittgenstein.
origin: The early Ludwig Wittgenstein's account of meaning in the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1921, 1922), on which a meaningful proposition is a logical picture of a possible state of affairs sharing its form.
